content: The expansion of community-based interventions for child development is essential to ensure that the benefits reach the largest number of disadvantaged children. This requires scaling up the implementation of the Care for Child Development (CCD) intervention through community-based providers, who are the backbone of primary healthcare in most low-income countries. Community health workers (CHWs) are already deeply involved in addressing the health and well-being of mothers and children. In many cases, CHWs are the only healthcare professionals families interact with during the early years of a child’s life, making them a critical point of contact for the majority of children in a community. Healthcare encounters with young children present unique opportunities to strengthen families’ efforts to promote their child’s development. These moments may be the only chance for healthcare providers in resource-limited settings to positively influence parents of young children. Therefore, integrating the CCD intervention into the existing work of community-based providers is crucial. This integration must be done in a way that does not impose an additional burden on these providers. Evidence from Pakistan’s Lady Health Workers program demonstrates that such integration is feasible. However, the intervention must be developed in close collaboration with existing community health worker programs, with a focus on providing adequate training, support, and motivation to healthcare providers. Organizations such as WHO, UNICEF, and their partners are actively advocating for the integration of the CCD intervention into existing health systems across all countries, with particular emphasis on poorly resourced areas. This approach aims to address the critical link between physical growth and psychological development in children, ensuring that interventions are both effective and sustainable.
